phonemes.desc: Voiceless alveolar stop [t] plus long close [eː] — the macron-marked length the ASCII form erases.
Voiceless alveolar fricative [s] — Classical Nahuatl z — with open [a].
Voiceless lateral affricate [tɬ] (tl) plus long close [iː].
Voiceless bilabial [p] plus long close-mid [oː], closing with open [a]; the stress falls on the long pō.

pronunciation.approximation: 'tehs-kaht-lee-POH-kah' — hold the first e and the lee long, with long ō on the stressed penult.

kin.label: His title
kin.form: Titlacahuan, 'We Are His Slaves' — the name his devotees used (Florentine Codex, Bk. 1)

kin.label: His glyph
kin.form: the obsidian mirror trailing smoke — a rebus drawn for the name in the codices, worn at the temple or replacing the lost foot

pronunciation.note: Tēzcatlīpōca is Tier 1: the macrons preserve the long vowels (ē, ī, ō) that ASCII flattens, per Karttunen's lexicon. The name compounds tēzcatl 'mirror' and pōca 'smoke' — the god's black glass is literally his name.

domains.title: The Smoking Mirror
domains.subtitle: Night, Sorcery, Strife, and the God-Impersonator
domains.lead: Tēzcatlīpōca is the Aztec night given will: the god of the obsidian mirror in which all things are seen, patron of rulers and sorcerers, tempter and destroyer of his own brother Quetzalcōātl. He is not evil — he is the shadow the world requires, and the Aztecs honored him with their most terrible beauty: the year-long god made flesh.

cards.name: The Mirror
cards.desc: Obsidian polished to black glass: it shows the future, the hidden, and the viewer's true face.

cards.name: The Missing Foot
cards.desc: Torn off by the earth-monster Cipactli in the creation — the mirror smokes where the foot was.

cards.name: The First Sun
cards.desc: He was the sun of the first age — the jaguar sun — devoured with his world when it ended.

cards.name: The Ixiptla
cards.desc: At Toxcatl, a flawless youth lived as the god for a year — then climbed the temple steps to die as him.

symbols.name: The smoking mirror
symbols.meaning: Knowledge of the hidden; the self seen without mercy

symbols.name: The jaguar
symbols.meaning: His nahual — the night's power and the first sun's ferocity

symbols.name: The missing foot
symbols.meaning: The price of creation: what the earth-monster took, and where the obsidian mirror now sits

symbols.name: The black stripe
symbols.meaning: The paint across his face — the night sky worn as war-color

mythology.lead: Tēzcatlīpōca's myths are all contest: with the earth-monster, with Quetzalcōātl, with the proud — he is the force that measures the strong by breaking them.

myths.title: The Foot in the Jaws
myths.text: To make the world, Tēzcatlīpōca and Quetzalcōātl descended to the primordial waters where the caiman-monster Cipactli floated, all mouths, snapping at every god who offered a limb. Tēzcatlīpōca gave his own foot as bait; the jaws closed on it — the sources preserve the detail that his foot, torn off, became the obsidian mirror that smokes — and in the moment the monster held him, the two gods seized her and tore her apart: her back became the earth, her eyes the springs, her mouth the cave from which humankind would emerge (Leyenda de los Soles; cf. Florentine Codex Bk. 7). Every Aztec king thereafter ruled over ground purchased with the god's flesh, and every sorcerer's mirror carried the same debt. The myth defines the god in a single stroke: the one who will pay a body-part to win a world, and who keeps, forever after, the gleaming proof of what it cost.

myths.title: The Jaguar Sun
myths.text: The Leyenda de los Soles counts the ages: the first was Four Jaguar, Nahui Ocēlōtl, whose sun was Tēzcatlīpōca and whose people were giants; the second Four Wind, whose sun was Quetzalcōātl; the third Four Rain, the sun of Tlāloc, ended in fire-rain; the fourth Four Water, the sun of Chalchiuhtlicue, ended in flood. The first age ended by fratricide: Quetzalcōātl struck Tēzcatlīpōca from the sky with a club, and jaguars devoured the giant people of the fallen world. Through the succession of suns the two brothers keep unmaking each other's worlds — the Aztec cosmos is their long quarrel, and the present Fifth Sun, Four Movement, is only the latest armistice, held together by sacrifice. The doctrine is stark: time itself is strife, every order is temporary, and the god of the smoking mirror is the one who reminds the others of it, age after age.

myths.title: The Mirror Trick
myths.text: Against Quetzalcōātl, priest-king of Tōllān, the night god came as a sorcerer. The sources differ in the details — the mirror in one telling, the enchanted pulque in another — but the sequence is constant: Tēzcatlīpōca showed the plumed god his own aged face in an obsidian mirror ('behold yourself, lord — your flesh is withered'), then broke him with drink until, shamed before his city, Quetzalcōātl burned his palace and departed eastward, immolating himself on a raft of serpents or sailing toward the dawn (Histoyre du Mechique; Anales de Cuauhtitlan). The Aztecs read the myth as the engine of history: Tēzcatlīpōca destroys every golden age, because every golden age conceals the strife that founded it, and he awaits his brother at every new shore. When the Spaniards came from the east, some wondered aloud which god had returned — and which had been waiting.

myths.title: Toxcatl
myths.text: Each year the Aztecs chose a flawless captive youth to be the ixiptla, the god's living image. For a year he walked as Tēzcatlīpōca: taught the flute, adorned, decked with flowers, given four maidens as wives in the names of four goddesses; through the streets he blessed the people — 'I am Tēzcatlīpōca, I am the god.' Twenty days before the end he was wed to the goddesses in the temple. At the feast of Toxcatl he climbed the temple steps breaking his flutes one by one, and at the summit his heart was offered to the night (Florentine Codex Bk. 2; Durán, Bk. 1). The friars who recorded it called it devilry and could not stop describing it: the most beautiful death in the Aztec year, and the empire's meditation on how divinity wears the flesh for a season and then puts it off — the god discarding, as he always does, what he has finished using.

lore.syncretism: The friars made him the devil — Sahagún's own informants struggle with the comparison — but the colonial fusion was subtler: he survived in Nahua sorcery as lord of the night and the crossroads, and in the dark side of the Day of the Dead. Scholars compare him with the disruptive, sovereignty-testing trickster found from Loki to Eshu: the power that governs by breaking. Modern Mexican letters reclaimed him as the national shadow — Octavio Paz's 'other Mexico,' the inward, night-facing double of every official sun. Guilhem Olivier's monograph made the point academically: to study Tēzcatlīpōca is to study how the Aztec state understood the necessity of its own negation.
lore.culturalLegacy: 'Smoking mirror' entered the world's vocabulary as the emblem of deceptive appearances. His obsidian mirror in the British Museum — Aztec-made, later owned by the Elizabethan magus John Dee as his scrying glass — is among the most storied objects on earth, linking Tenochtitlan to the court of Elizabeth I. Every account of Aztec civilization, from the earliest friars to the present, must reckon with his Toxcatl: the rite that made beauty, divinity, and death one ceremony. In Mexico his name still brands nightclubs, football chants, and political cartoons — the god of the untouchable shadow, as serviceable to the modern state as to the empire that fed him hearts.
lore.extendedMeditation: Tēzcatlīpōca is the god of the honest mirror. He flatters no one: he shows the king his age, the golden age its end, the world its price. Every tradition needs a power that tests rather than comforts; the Aztecs gave him their most beautiful ceremonies, understanding that what breaks you falsely was never yours — and what survives the mirror is. He is the night's argument that the state carries with it always: legitimacy is not a possession but an examination, renewed every age, and the examiner has one black eye of volcanic glass and no mercy in it.
sources: Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Bks. 1–2 (the god; the Toxcatl festival)
Leyenda de los Soles (Codex Chimalpopoca; the suns and the creation)
Histoyre du Mechique; Anales de Cuauhtitlan (the fall of Tollan)
Durán, Book of the Gods and Rites, Bk. 1 (Toxcatl)
Karttunen, An Analytical Dictionary of Nahuatl, s.v. tēzcatl, pōca
Olivier, Guilhem, Mockeries and Metamorphoses of an Aztec God (2003)
lore.archaeology: His obsidian mirrors survive across collections — the British Museum's Dee mirror foremost — ground from the volcanic glass that Pachuca and Otumba supplied by the ton. The Florentine Codex's account of Toxcatl, illustrated by Nahua artists under Sahagún, is the fullest ritual description from the pre-Columbian world. Templo Mayor excavations found his cult's material traces among the offerings, and the Calendar Stone's jaguar-sun glyph keeps his first age on the empire's central monument. The ixiptla's flutes themselves survive in museum cases — small clay instruments, some broken exactly as the rite demanded.
lore.originalScriptNote: In Aztec writing the name is a rebus: the smoking mirror itself — the obsidian disc with its scroll of smoke — worn at his temple or replacing his torn-off foot. The codices draw the name rather than spell it: the smoking mirror is both his glyph and his body.
